June 15, 2026 
 
The Honorable Robert Kennedy, Jr.  
Secretary Department of Health and Human Services  
200 Independence Avenue SW  
Washington, DC 20201  
 
The Honorable Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services  
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services  
200 Independence Avenue SW  
Washington, DC 20201 
 
 
Re: 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed 
rule (CMS-0062-P). 
 
Dear Secretary Kennedy and Administrator Oz: 
 
Blood Cancer United appreciates the opportunity to provide comment on the Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule.  At Blood Cancer United, our 
mission is to cure blood cancer and improve the quality of life of all patients and their 
families. To achieve it, we unite a community of people—patients and their families, 
volunteers, healthcare providers, scientists, staff, partners, fundraisers, and philanthropists—
who believe all blood cancer patients deserve longer, fuller lives. We fund innovative 
research, offer free resources and personalized support, and advocate at the state and 
national levels for more accessible and affordable healthcare for all patients.  
 
Prior authorization significantly impacts blood cancer patients by causing delays in accessing 
necessary treatments, which is critical for these patients, as timely therapy can dramatically 
affect outcomes in blood cancers.1 Prior authorization remains a major challenge for patients 
and an onerous process for providers, diverting valuable resources away from direct care and 
delaying access to needed services and treatment. Furthermore, improper prior authorization 
denials and prolonged response times cause delays and/or abandonment of necessary 
health care services, treatment, and medications.2 We are pleased to see the administration is 
continuing efforts to modernize the prior authorization process. We offer the following 
 
1 Chino, F., Baez, A., Elkins, I. B., Aviki, E. M., Ghazal, L. V., & Thom, B. (2023). The Patient Experience of Prior Authorization for 
Cancer Care. JAMA Network Open, 6(10), e2338182. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.38182 
2 Ashley Kirzinger, Julian Montalvo III, and Liz Hamel “KFF Health Tracking Poll: Prior Authorizations Rank as Public’s Biggest 
Burden When Getting Health Care,” KFF. February 2026. Accessed at: https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/kff-health-tracking-poll-
prior-authorizations-rank-as-publics-biggest-burden-when-getting-health-care/  
 
 
comments on specific provisions in the proposed rule, and recommendations for additional 
policies the agency can implement to improve the patient health care experience. 
 
Extending Electronic Prior Authorization Standards to Prescription Drugs 
Prescription drugs are often a key component of care for individuals with chronic health 
conditions who are prescribed complex drug regimens that need to be managed to ensure 
they are best suited for the individual and to avoid drug interactions. Continuing to exclude 
prescription drugs from electronic prior authorization standards will result in a significant 
burden to providers and patients who must manage multiple systems in order to ensure that 
the patient has access to medically appropriate treatments.   
 
Blood Cancer United therefore strongly supports the proposal to extend prior authorization 
application programming interface (API) requirements to prescription drugs, regardless of 
whether they are covered under a plan’s medical or pharmacy benefit. CMS should also 
require real-time identification of the applicable benefit pathway and greater consistency in 
terminology, documentation requirements, and workflows across medical-benefit and 
pharmacy-benefit drugs. Patients and providers should not experience delays because a 
request was routed incorrectly or because responsibility for the authorization is unclear. 
 
However, inclusion of prescription drugs in electronic prior authorization standards alone will 
not fully address the longstanding challenges patients face in accessing medications. 
Electronic modernization should improve the timeliness and appropriateness of coverage 
decisions, not simply accelerate existing utilization-management practices. CMS should 
ensure that automated tools do not result in inappropriate denials or replace meaningful 
clinical review. Denials involving complex treatment decisions should be reviewed by an 
appropriately qualified clinician. CMS should also monitor denial and overturn rates to 
identify patterns that may indicate inappropriate utilization-management practices.  
 
Many people with chronic health conditions take the same medications for decades, yet still 
face “prior” authorization to continue taking these medications. Enrollees and physicians 
consistently report yearly or “surprise” prior authorization requirements for medications that 
the enrollee is already taking. Enrollees often only discover a new prior authorization 
requirement when they contact the pharmacy for a refill, risking a gap in care. Such gaps in 
care can lead to an exacerbation of symptoms or avoidable emergency department visits. 
CMS should establish guardrails to prevent unnecessary repeat prior authorization for 
medications, including prohibiting reauthorization for patients stable on long-term therapies, 
requiring approvals to remain valid for the duration of treatment, and preventing new prior 
authorization requirements from being imposed mid-course without continuity protections. 
Continuity-of-care protections should also apply when an enrollee changes plans or coverage 
types. CMS should require plans to honor existing approvals for an appropriate transition 
period and ensure that relevant authorization history is transferred between payers so that 
patients are not required to restart authorization, documentation, or appeals processes 
 
 
unnecessarily. Where applicable, plans should also honor prior step-therapy exceptions and 
avoid requiring patients to repeat therapies that were previously ineffective or inappropriate. 
 
Extending Electronic Prior Authorization Standards to the Small Group Market 
We strongly support the proposal to extend electronic prior authorization standards to 
insurers selling plans to small employers buying coverage in the federally facilitated Small 
Business Health Options Program (FF-SHOP). As CMS notes in the proposed rule, all insurers 
that offer small-group market QHPs on the FF-SHOPs also offer individual-market QHPs on 
the FFM. The burden on FF-SHOP insurers would therefore be minimal, since they are 
already required to implement the policies for their individual market QHPs and the benefit 
to patients who obtain their coverage through a SHOP plan would be substantial. We also 
encourage CMS to continue exploring opportunities to promote more consistent prior 
authorization protections across coverage markets. Patients should not face substantially 
different processes, timelines, or continuity-of-care protections based solely on the type of 
coverage they hold. 
 
New Timeframe Requirements for QHP Issuers to Notify Providers 
We appreciate CMS requiring QHP issuers  to respond to prior authorization requests for 
non-drug items and services in shorter timeframes than currently apply, consistent with those 
that apply to other payers, that is, no later than 7 days for standard requests and no later than 
72 hours for expedited requests. However, as we noted in our comments on the 2024 
proposed rule, we expect the efficiencies created by the automated process to make shorter 
timeframes possible. Specifically, we recommend that standard requests should be resolved 
within 72 hours and expedited requests within 24 hours. Individuals with chronic illnesses are 
frequently harmed by unnecessary delays in receiving medical treatments.  
 
CMS additionally proposes that insurers may extend the timeframes to notify the requesting 
provider of a prior authorization decision by up to 14 calendar days under certain 
circumstances. We recommend limiting extensions to 168 hours (the equivalent of 7 days). 
CMS should also require that patients and providers receive a notice of extension when an 
insurer requests one and the specific basis for the extension.  
 
With regard to timeframes for QHP issuers to respond to prior authorization requests for 
prescription drugs, we urge CMS to require insurers to respond within 24 hours in all cases, 
rather than the proposed timeframes of no later than 72 hours for standard requests and 24 
hours for expedited requests. This would align the timeframes for QHP enrollees with those 
that apply to Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) plans.   
 
Additionally, CMS should require that prior authorization be valid for the duration of 
treatment and/or set limits on the possible frequency of prior authorization requirements. 
Individuals with stable diagnoses and long-term treatment needs should not have to renew 
prior authorization on, for example, a monthly basis. This is a waste of resources for enrollees 
and providers, and sometimes leads to treatment gaps that are avoidable. CMS should also 
 
 
explicitly extend these protections to ensure continuity of care when individuals switch plans, 
such that existing prior authorizations remain valid for a reasonable transition period and do 
not require unnecessary reauthorization that could disrupt ongoing treatment. 
 
Finally, to ensure that applicable timelines are meaningful and enforceable, we recommend 
that a failure by the responsible entity to issue a determination within the prescribed 
timeframe be treated as a “deemed denial,” thereby triggering the beneficiary’s right to 
appeal. Without such consequences, timelines risk being aspirational rather than binding. 
This framework would preserve procedural protections for beneficiaries by enabling timely 
escalation, while still maintaining the integrity of the review process.  
 
Reporting API Usage Metrics 
We support CMS’s expansion of required API usage metrics and believe the data will be 
beneficial to learning how APIs are being used by providers and payers. CMS should collect 
disaggregated data by provider type, plan, organizational size, and geographic regions. 
Even if this data is not shared publicly, as CMS has proposed, disaggregating data will allow 
CMS to identify disparities in patient access to health data. 
 
However, we strongly urge CMS to make API usage data publicly available and to post it 
routinely—at least annually—for various stakeholders to access. Publication of this data would 
benefit patients, policymakers, and other stakeholders with an interest in API usage and help 
inform efforts to increase use by providers or patients, or take action on other trends 
identified from the data.  
 
Reporting API Endpoints and URL/Centralized Directory 
We strongly support the proposal to require impacted payers to report their Patient Access, 
Provider Directory, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization API endpoints to 
CMS.  
 
We continue to support the electronic health data-sharing and prior authorization initiatives 
and are hopeful for the expansion of these systems. We believe that a centralized endpoint 
directory maintained by CMS is crucial to the longevity and sustainability of the API use. By 
maintaining a public, open, and easily accessible directory of API endpoints, CMS ensures 
that endpoint information pertinent to the building and operation of interoperable API 
systems remains freely available rather than monetized or restricted. We also believe this 
directory will help researchers and patient advocates understand the information used in 
coverage decisions.  
 
As the agency responsible for overseeing these interoperability initiatives, CMS is more than 
suited to maintain this directory. This proposal is an important example of the role the 
government can serve in upholding transparency, facilitating information sharing, and 
supporting technological systems to improve patient health care access.  
 
 
 
 
Updated Website Reporting  
We strongly support the additional requirements for reporting on prior authorization metrics, 
and we appreciate that CMS has proposed to extend these requirements to prescription 
drug prior authorization requests. The newly proposed requirement to report the total 
number of prior authorization requests and outcomes, combined with the reported 
percentages, will allow patients, researchers, and policymakers to understand the prevalence 
and likelihood of approvals, denials, and appeals for standard, expedited, and extended-
timeframe requests.  
 
Despite these advancements, the current reporting requirements mask key information about 
the populations impacted by prior authorization. CMS should require that reporting data be 
disaggregated by factors including service type, provider type, diagnosis, geography, 
income, disability, gender, race and ethnicity, and age. It is important for our patients and 
their advocates to know where prior authorization requests are being submitted, for which 
health conditions, and to which patients.  
 
A significant barrier to accessing prior authorization reporting is the lack of consistency in 
website location, publication format, and terminology.3 We encourage CMS to standardize 
where data are displayed on insurer websites and to standardize the file type and layout of 
prior authorization reports so that patients, policymakers, and other stakeholders can more 
easily find and analyze published data. Standardization would also allow for easier 
comparison across health plans, states, insurers, and coverage programs. CMS should also 
consider creating a centralized, searchable public dashboard so that patients, providers, 
researchers, and policymakers can more easily compare prior authorization practices across 
plans and coverage programs.  
 
CMS should also require reporting on measures that more directly reflect the patient 
experience, including overturn rates, the frequency of repeat prior authorization requests, 
expedited-review outcomes, authorization outcomes following plan transitions, and, where 
feasible, the time between submission of a request and receipt of the prescribed treatment. 
Reporting should also capture step-therapy-related delays and outcomes. These measures 
would help patients, providers, advocates, and policymakers evaluate whether prior 
authorization practices are delaying or disrupting access to care. 
 
Strengthen Prior Authorization Determination Explanations  
We appreciate that both in this proposed rule and in the 2024 Interoperability rule, CMS 
requires that all prior authorization determinations–those conducted by electronic portals, 
email, fax, or telephone–include a specific reason for denied prior authorization decisions. 
 
3 Kaye Pestaina, “Insurers’ Prior Authorization Data Offers Little Insight Into What Gets Approved or Denied,” KFF. April 2026. 
Accessed at https://www.kff.org/quick-insights/insurers-prior-authorization-data-offers-little-insight-into-what-gets-approved-or-
denied/  
 
 
We urge CMS to further strengthen these requirements by requiring greater specificity in 
denial determinations. 
 
Denial determinations should provide sufficient detail into the rationale for the decision to 
enable patients and providers to take action. For example, denials due to missing supporting 
documentation should clearly stipulate the necessary documents for proper review. Denials 
based on “medical necessity” could cover a wide range of potential factors. States, plans, and 
QHP insurers should be obligated to provide a more granular response than “failure to 
establish medical necessity.” CMS should require insurers to explicitly state the coverage 
policy or clinical criteria standard used to determine a denial, and provide information on 
covered alternatives. This information would better inform patients and providers of their 
next steps. 
 
Denial notices should also be written in plain language and include standardized instructions 
for requesting reconsideration or filing an appeal, including applicable timelines, deadlines, 
and clear next steps. Patients and providers should receive notice at the same time. CMS 
should also require appropriate language-access and accessibility standards so that patients 
and caregivers can understand the decision and take timely action. 
 
Request For Information: Laboratory Tests and Durable Medical Equipment, 
Prosthetics, Orthotics, and Supplies Items (DMEPOS)  
We are pleased to see CMS is considering how prior authorization requirements for 
laboratory tests and Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics, and Supplies 
(DMEPOS) items impact patients and what changes could be made to improve patient 
outcomes.  
 
Delays in laboratory testing due to prior authorization requirements can stall notice of a 
patient’s health status, impede medical diagnoses, and postpone the next steps in treatment 
planning. CMS should ensure that patients have a clear understanding of the materials 
required for their prior authorization requests, including knowledge of whether a laboratory 
is in-network or out-of-network. CMS should ensure that providers and laboratories receive 
timely updates on prior authorization requests regardless of a lab’s in-network or out-of-
network status. 
 
Similarly, prior authorization can create barriers for patients in need of medical equipment, 
prosthetics, orthotics, and mobility devices, hindering their ability to maintain independence. 
Patients seeking to attain DMEPOS are often denied when an insurer deems a device 
medically unnecessary. Due to individual needs and the specificity of prosthetics and other 
devices, CMS should require states, plans, and QHP issuers to clearly articulate the standard 
used to determine medical necessity and provide detailed information on how to navigate 
appeals. 
 
Encouraging Provider Adoption of APIs  
 
 
For patients to receive the most from the 2020, 2024, and proposed 2026 Interoperability 
rules, providers must have the technological systems necessary to support electronic prior 
authorization and APIs. CMS’s proposal to collect Provider Access API usage data will provide 
greater insight into how widely electronic prior authorization is being adopted. 
 
Recent data shows that many providers and provider organizations have not adopted 
electronic prior authorization systems. While 90 percent of medical plans have reported 
starting to implement required APIs by the January 1, 2027, deadline, providers are 
significantly further behind, with only 33 percent indicating that they are likely to implement 
the Provider Access API.4 Providers identify limited funding, lack of internal expertise, and 
challenges coordinating with vendors and health plans as barriers to implementation.5 
 
We encourage CMS to explore ways to facilitate greater uptake of API use among providers 
by, for example, looking at the successful effort to boost provider adoption of the electronic 
generation of prescriptions (e-prescribing) and electronic health record (EHR) systems.6,7 
CMS should also consider using the recently announced Electronic Prior Authorization 
Acceleration initiative to develop pilot programs specifically designed to educate medical 
practices, especially small and medium-sized organizations, and provide guidance on 
developing, implementing, and operating new technological systems.8 
 
 
 
Conclusion 
Blood Cancer United thanks CMS again for its leadership in this important area and this 
opportunity to provide comment on this proposed rule. If you have any questions or would 
like to discuss our comments further, please contact Phil Waters, Director, Federal Public 
Policy at Blood Cancer United at phil.waters@bloodcancerunited.org.  
 
 
 
Sincerely,

https://ﬁles.constantcontact.com/cc5af31a201/19d6312d-b5c5-438e-bdd2-b504f724eb4e.pdf

Program,” Health Affairs. July 2013. Accessed at https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2012.1197 
7 Clemens Scott Kruse et al., “Adoption Factors of the Electronic Health Record: A Systematic Review” JMIR Med Inform 
2016;4(2):e19. Accessed at: https://medinform.jmir.org/2016/2/e19

authorization-accelerating-momentum    
 
 
 
 
Bethany Lilly 
Executive Director, Public Policy

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Blood Cancer United; signed by Bethany Lilly, Executive Director, Public Policy.
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group; patient advocacy organization.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Nonprofit focused on curing blood cancer, improving quality of life for patients and families, funding research, providing patient support, and advocating for accessible and affordable healthcare.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Blood Cancer United strongly supports extending electronic prior authorization standards to prescription drugs under both medical and pharmacy benefits and extending requirements to FF-SHOP small group plans. It urges CMS to go further by requiring clearer benefit-pathway identification, faster timeframes, stronger denial explanations, continuity-of-care protections, public and disaggregated reporting, centralized endpoint directories and dashboards, and greater provider API adoption.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; API-USAGE-METRICS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; GENERAL/RFIs.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** Not specifically cited by CFR section; references CMS-0062-P and prior 2024 Interoperability rule.
- **Standards referenced:** Prior Authorization APIs; Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization API endpoints; electronic PA; EHR and provider adoption; e-prescribing.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Extend electronic PA to prescription drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Prescription drugs are central to chronic and complex care, including cancer treatment, and excluding them from ePA standards forces providers and patients to manage multiple systems.
- **Specific request:** Finalize extension to drugs under both medical and pharmacy benefits; require real-time identification of the benefit pathway and consistent terminology, documentation, and workflows.

**Topic 2: Guardrails against inappropriate PA and repeat authorization**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Electronic modernization should not merely accelerate inappropriate denials or longstanding utilization-management barriers.
- **Specific request:** Require qualified clinician review for complex denials, monitor denial and overturn rates, prohibit unnecessary repeat PA for stable long-term therapies, make approvals valid for duration of treatment, and protect continuity when enrollees change plans.

**Topic 3: FF-SHOP extension**
- **Provision ID:** FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Small-group FF-SHOP issuers already offering individual-market QHPs should have minimal incremental burden, while patients in SHOP plans would benefit substantially.
- **Specific request:** Finalize FF-SHOP extension and continue promoting consistent PA protections across coverage markets.

**Topic 4: Prior authorization timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Chronic illness patients are harmed by delays, and electronic efficiencies should permit shorter timeframes.
- **Specific request:** Require 72 hours for standard and 24 hours for expedited non-drug requests; limit extensions to 7 days; require notice and basis for extensions; require 24-hour responses for all QHP prescription drug PA; treat missed deadlines as deemed denials triggering appeal rights.

**Topic 5: API usage metrics and transparency**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Usage metrics can reveal adoption and disparities, but public and disaggregated reporting is needed for accountability.
- **Specific request:** Collect disaggregated API usage data by provider type, plan, organizational size, and geography; make data public at least annually.

**Topic 6: Endpoint reporting and centralized directory**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** A CMS-maintained public endpoint directory prevents endpoint information from becoming restricted or monetized and supports researchers and advocates.
- **Specific request:** Finalize endpoint reporting for Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and PA APIs and maintain an open centralized directory.

**Topic 7: Prior authorization reporting metrics and public website reporting**
- **Provision ID:** TRANSPARENCY; API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Current reporting masks the populations and services affected by PA and is difficult to locate or compare.
- **Specific request:** Require disaggregation by service type, provider type, diagnosis, geography, income, disability, gender, race/ethnicity, and age; standardize website location, file type, layout, terminology; create a centralized searchable dashboard; add patient-experience measures.

**Topic 8: Denial explanations**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Generic denial reasons like “medical necessity” do not help patients or providers correct, appeal, or understand decisions.
- **Specific request:** Require detailed denial rationales, missing-document identification, policy/clinical criteria used, covered alternatives, plain language, appeal instructions, simultaneous notice to patients/providers, and language-access/accessibility standards.

**Topic 9: Lab tests and DMEPOS RFI**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFIs
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** PA delays for lab testing and DMEPOS can impede diagnosis, treatment planning, independence, and access to medically necessary equipment.
- **Specific request:** Ensure patients understand required materials and network status; require timely updates for providers/labs; require clear medical necessity standards and appeals information for DMEPOS.

**Topic 10: Provider API adoption**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Provider adoption is far behind payer implementation, threatening the practical value of APIs.
- **Specific request:** Use API usage data, incentives, pilots, education, and support modeled on e-prescribing/EHR adoption to increase provider uptake, especially among small and medium practices.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12/S15/S21:** Strongly supports extending PA APIs to drugs and requests real-time benefit-pathway identification and workflow consistency.
- **S16/S17:** Requests stronger, more specific denial explanations including missing documentation, clinical criteria, covered alternatives, appeal instructions, and accessibility standards.
- **S20/S43:** Requests shorter PA timeframes, especially 24-hour QHP drug determinations, and enforceability through deemed denial if deadlines are missed.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** Supports API usage metrics but requests public, annual, disaggregated reporting.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Strongly supports endpoint reporting and a centralized CMS directory.
- **S40-S42:** Strongly supports extending requirements to FF-SHOP plans, arguing burden is minimal and patient benefit substantial.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to lab/DMEPOS and provider adoption themes, requesting patient-centered protections and support for API adoption.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize ePA standards for prescription drugs under both medical and pharmacy benefits.
2. Require real-time identification of whether the medical or pharmacy benefit pathway applies.
3. Require consistent terminology, documentation, and workflows across benefit types.
4. Require qualified clinician review of complex denials and monitor denial/overturn patterns.
5. Prohibit unnecessary repeat PA for patients stable on long-term therapies.
6. Require PA approvals to remain valid for the duration of treatment and through plan transitions for an appropriate period.
7. Finalize FF-SHOP extension.
8. Shorten non-drug PA timeframes to 72 hours standard and 24 hours expedited.
9. Require all QHP prescription drug PA decisions within 24 hours.
10. Limit extensions to 7 days and require notice to patients/providers.
11. Treat missed deadlines as deemed denials that trigger appeal rights.
12. Make API usage data public, annual, and disaggregated.
13. Maintain a public CMS endpoint directory.
14. Standardize PA reporting websites, formats, and terminology and create a centralized dashboard.
15. Strengthen denial explanation content and accessibility requirements.
16. Support provider API adoption through pilots, guidance, education, and incentives.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** PA delays for blood cancer and chronic illness patients; inappropriate denials; repeat PA for stable therapies; unclear benefit routing; insufficient transparency; weak provider API adoption.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Treatment delays, medication abandonment, emergency department visits, gaps in care, repeated therapies after plan changes, inability to appeal effectively, and disparities hidden by aggregate data.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Provider lack of funding and expertise, vendor/health plan coordination challenges, inconsistent website reporting, and fragmented PA processes across coverage types.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** WEDI survey stating 90% of medical plans reported starting API implementation by January 1, 2027, while only 33% of providers indicated likely Provider Access API implementation.
- **Studies or research referenced:** JAMA Network Open study on patient experience of PA for cancer care; KFF poll identifying PA as a major burden; KFF analysis on insurer PA data; Health Affairs e-prescribing adoption study; JMIR EHR adoption systematic review; CMS early adopters press release.
- **Examples provided:** Patients stable on medications facing yearly or surprise PA; refill gaps discovered at the pharmacy; repeated step therapy after plan changes; lab/DMEPOS delays.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Blood cancer patients, chronic illness patients, caregivers, providers, QHP enrollees, small group plan enrollees, researchers, patient advocates, payers, labs, DMEPOS suppliers, and small/medium providers.
- **Economic implications:** Reduced duplicate PA and clearer reporting could lower administrative burden; provider adoption may require funding, pilots, and support.
- **Technical feasibility:** Supports APIs but stresses real-time pathway routing, consistent reporting infrastructure, and provider-side technology adoption.
- **Patient care impact:** High. Comment repeatedly emphasizes that delays in cancer and chronic disease treatment can materially affect outcomes.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with patient-protective modifications.
- **Tone:** Professional, patient-centered, advocacy-oriented.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Blood Cancer United therefore strongly supports the proposal to extend prior authorization application programming interface (API) requirements to prescription drugs." - Context: Support for drug ePA extension.
2. "Electronic modernization should improve the timeliness and appropriateness of coverage decisions, not simply accelerate existing utilization-management practices." - Context: Concern about automation without clinical safeguards.
3. "Patients and providers should not experience delays because a request was routed incorrectly or because responsibility for the authorization is unclear." - Context: Medical vs pharmacy pathway clarity.
4. "Without such consequences, timelines risk being aspirational rather than binding." - Context: Request for deemed denial if timeframes are missed.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Requests shorter decision timeframes and enforceability.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Discusses provider adoption barriers including funding and expertise.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Highlights burden on providers managing multiple PA systems and documentation.
- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not a major theme.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Requests disaggregation by demographic and socioeconomic factors to identify disparities.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Addresses provider API adoption and real-time pathway identification.
- [ ] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Standards maturity is not a central issue.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central theme; delays in cancer and chronic disease care are emphasized throughout.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not addressed.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Emphasizes patients, providers, payers, researchers, advocates, and CMS directory roles.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Requests real-time pathway identification and consistent workflows.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Strong focus on denial explanations, public metrics, dashboards, and endpoint directories.
- [ ] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not addressed as small payer impact, though FF-SHOP burden is discussed.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Discusses current PA, refill, step therapy, lab, DMEPOS, and provider workflow barriers.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Notes provider/vendor/plan coordination challenges for API adoption.
